design_detail: Cross-sectional family study (a Science report without section headings). 50 biological sibling pairs, in each of which one sibling met DSM-IV criteria for stimulant dependence and the other had no history of chronic drug or alcohol abuse (the paper's inclusion criterion), compared with 50 unrelated healthy volunteers matched for age and IQ. Measures: stop-signal reaction time (SSRT); white-matter fractional anisotropy (FA) from diffusion tensor imaging, analysed with tract-based spatial statistics; grey-matter volume by voxel-based morphometry (both in FSL). Familiality was tested by permutation: whether a trait varied less within true sibling pairs than within randomly re-paired participants. Recorded as cross-sectional rather than case-control (the abstract-based draft) because participants were selected on dependence status, the exposure, and compared at a single time. The main report (pp. 601–604) was read in full; its Supporting Online Material (methods, figs. S1–S2, tables S1–S3), which holds the sample characteristics, drug-use data and imaging statistics, is not in the PDF and was not read. Locators count the report's running-text paragraphs from the first one after the abstract.
can_establish: Whether stop-signal and brain-structure differences seen in people with stimulant dependence are also present in their siblings who were not dependent, and whether these traits are more alike within families than between unrelated people, which points to a familial (genetic or shared-environment) component.
cannot_establish: That the shared differences predate drug use in the dependent siblings (nobody was assessed before use began); that they are genetic rather than due to the shared family environment (siblings share both); that stimulant use has no effect of its own (shared differences could still be worsened by use, and the main report does not compare the dependent with the non-dependent siblings directly); or anything specific to methamphetamine (the main report does not say which stimulants were used).

sample.recruitment: Not described in the main report (methods are in the supplement, not read). The acknowledgments thank the clinical study officers of the Mental Health Research Network for help with volunteer recruitment (p. 604).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: One sibling of each pair met DSM-IV criteria for dependence on stimulant drugs; the other had no history of chronic drug or alcohol abuse; controls were unrelated healthy volunteers (p. 602, 3rd paragraph). Further criteria are in the supplement (not read).
sample.demographics: Not given in the main report. Controls were matched to the sibling pairs for age and IQ (table S1, not read); sex and education are not reported in the main text. Smoking rates were higher in the sibling pairs than in the controls (p. 602; rates in table S1).
sample.attrition: Not reported. The F tests for SSRT and FA have 2 and 141 degrees of freedom, which implies 144 participants analysed rather than 150; who was left out, and why, is not stated in the main text (p. 602, Fig. 1 legend).
sample.selection_effects: Families in which a sibling free of chronic drug or alcohol problems agreed to take part beside a dependent sibling: dependent people with such a sibling may differ from those without, and the non-dependent siblings are a selected group (the authors suggest they have resilience factors, p. 604). Controls were volunteers matched only on age and IQ. Smoking was more common in both sibling groups than in the controls.

exposure.measurement: DSM-IV diagnosis of stimulant dependence (p. 602); the diagnostic instrument and any biological verification are described only in the supplement. The main report does not say which stimulants the dependent siblings used; a later review states that most used cocaine (Dean et al., 2013, p. 263).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not in the main report. Duration of stimulant use appears only as a correlate within the dependent group (figs. S2A–B, not read).
exposure.polysubstance: Not described in the main report beyond tobacco: smoking was more common in both sibling groups, and an analysis restricted to non-smokers gave similar grey-matter results (fig. S1, not read; p. 603). No such check is reported for FA or SSRT. Alcohol and other drug use of the dependent siblings is not described in the main text.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported in the main report: whether the dependent siblings were using, in treatment or abstinent when scanned is not stated.

comparison.controls: 50 unrelated healthy volunteers (p. 602); within families, the non-dependent biological siblings.
comparison.matching: Controls matched to the sibling pairs for age and IQ (p. 602; table S1, not read). Sex and education are not reported in the main text.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No assessment before drug use began in the dependent siblings. The non-dependent sibling stands in for the pre-use state, which assumes that both siblings started alike; genes and the shared family environment (for example adversity or parental substance use) are not separated.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Non-dependent siblings: no history of chronic drug or alcohol abuse, so occasional use is not excluded by the stated criterion. Unrelated controls: described as healthy; their drug and alcohol use is not reported in the main text.

outcomes.instruments: Stop-signal task (SSRT); diffusion tensor imaging with tract-based spatial statistics (FA) and voxel-based morphometry (grey-matter volume) in FSL; a right inferior frontal and pre-supplementary motor region of interest from Hammers' probabilistic atlas for the FA–SSRT regression; permutation tests of within-pair similarity (p. 602).
outcomes.validity_norms: SSRT is a standard laboratory measure of response inhibition; it is compared with the control group, not with norms. The imaging measures are group-relative.
outcomes.operationalization: An abnormality is a difference from the unrelated controls; a difference is called familial when it varies less within true sibling pairs than within random pairs; impaired self-control means a longer SSRT than the controls.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Three outcome measures (SSRT, FA, grey-matter volume), the last two tested voxel by voxel. Bonferroni correction for the two SSRT comparisons with controls (P ≤ 0.005 for both; Fig. 1A legend). The correction applied to the voxel-wise FA and grey-matter maps is described only in the supplement (not read). The six familiality permutation tests are reported without correction; editors' calculation: across six tests a Bonferroni threshold would be P < 0.0083, which the SSRT (0.033), putamen (0.013) and posterior insula (0.012) results do not meet.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; the imaging analyses are automated.

analysis.effect_sizes: No standardized effect sizes or cluster statistics in the main report. SSRT: group difference F(2,141) = 9.9, P < 0.001; both sibling groups slower than the controls (Bonferroni P ≤ 0.005); read from Fig. 1A (approximate; the error bars are not defined in the legend): controls about 239 ms, non-dependent siblings about 277 ms, dependent siblings about 280 ms. FA: group difference in the tract skeleton F(2,141) = 26.3, P < 0.001. FA beside the right inferior frontal gyrus against SSRT, all participants pooled: r = 0.24 printed without sign (the text and Fig. 1C describe higher FA with shorter SSRT, a negative relation), R² = 0.057, P < 0.005. Familiality (permutation): SSRT P = 0.033; FA P = 0.004; right prefrontal white matter P = 0.004; putamen enlargement P = 0.013; posterior insula reduction P = 0.012; amygdala enlargement P = 0.144 (not familial). Editors' calculation from the F statistics, η² = 2F/(2F + 141): about 0.12 for SSRT and 0.27 for FA; the FA value may be too large if the skeleton voxels were chosen because they differed between groups (see reporting issues).
analysis.covariates: Not stated in the main report (supplement not read). Controls matched for age and IQ; tobacco addressed only by the non-smoker re-analysis of grey matter (fig. S1, not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: The main report names only the grey-matter clusters shared by both sibling groups and the regions tested for familiality. Fig. 2A shows decreased-volume clusters in the dependent group, in ventral frontal and insular regions by the editors' reading of the figure, that are absent from the siblings' map (Fig. 2B), and Fig. 2B shows large increased-volume clusters in the posterior fossa of the siblings (the cerebellum, by the editors' reading); neither is named or discussed. No direct comparison of the dependent with the non-dependent siblings is reported, so whether any difference is specific to the dependent siblings cannot be tested from the main report. The correlations with duration of stimulant use, the cluster statistics and the correction method are only in the supplement.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Both siblings of each pair had longer SSRT and lower white-matter FA than unrelated controls, and they shared three grey-matter differences from the controls (larger left amygdala and left putamen; smaller left postcentral gyrus, superior temporal gyrus and posterior insula). SSRT, FA, right prefrontal FA, putamen and posterior insula varied less within families than between random pairs; the amygdala did not. In the dependent siblings, lower FA went with longer stimulant use (supplement, not read).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the findings support an underlying neurocognitive endophenotype for stimulant addiction (p. 601). The text goes further: poor inhibitory control is called a familial trait and not a result of long-term drug use (p. 602), the right prefrontal FA finding is called an objective vulnerability marker (p. 602), and the grey-matter and white-matter changes are said to underlie an increased risk of dependence (p. 604). Gaps: (1) an endophenotype must be heritable, but siblings share environment as well as genes and no heritability was estimated; the authors themselves note that an equal SSRT deficit in both siblings does not fit the classic endophenotype pattern of relatives falling between patients and controls (p. 604); (2) an equal deficit in a non-dependent sibling shows that the trait is shared, not that drug use adds nothing or that the trait came first; (3) 'underlie' and 'vulnerability marker' are causal or predictive readings of cross-sectional data; (4) the marker rests on r = 0.24 (about 6% of SSRT variance) across all participants pooled, which mixes the between-group difference with individual variation; (5) the abstract speaks of fronto-striatal systems, but the grey-matter differences shared by both siblings lie in the amygdala, putamen, posterior insula and adjacent parietal and temporal cortex, and the frontal finding is white matter beside the right inferior frontal gyrus.

timeline.event: The same group's earlier sibling study reported higher Barratt impulsivity scores and normal sensation-seeking in non-dependent siblings (Ersche et al., 2010, Biological Psychiatry, as cited on p. 604; not read).
This study: SSRT, FA and grey-matter differences shared by 50 sibling pairs discordant for stimulant dependence.
Review notes that most participants in this sibling study used cocaine rather than methamphetamine

Review summarizes the brain findings, adding a hippocampal enlargement in both siblings and orbitofrontal and anterior insular reductions in the dependent siblings only, none of which is named in the main report

replication.where_it_stands: No direct replication of this sibling design has been read for the encyclopedia; the status records the project's reading, not a search of the literature. The study is the encyclopedia's main human evidence that some brain and stop-signal differences seen in stimulant dependence are shared with non-dependent siblings; it says nothing specific about methamphetamine.

funding.funder: UK Medical Research Council; conducted in the Behavioural and Clinical Neuroscience Institute, University of Cambridge, jointly funded by the MRC and the Wellcome Trust; three authors supported by an MRC research grant (p. 604, Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: T.W.R. and A.J.T. consult for Cambridge Cognition; E.T.B. is employed half-time by GlaxoSmithKline and half-time by the University of Cambridge; K.D.E., P.S.J. and G.B.W. declare no conflicts (p. 604).
funding.affiliations_note: University of Cambridge (Behavioural and Clinical Neuroscience Institute, Experimental Psychology, Psychiatry, Wolfson Brain Imaging Centre), GlaxoSmithKline Clinical Unit Cambridge, and Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS Foundation Trust (p. 602). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective family cohort that images and tests children or adolescents before any drug use and follows them and their siblings through the ages of onset, so that differences present before use can be separated from changes after it; a twin design would also separate genetic from shared-environment effects. Meanwhile, a direct contrast of dependent with non-dependent siblings, reported with cluster statistics, would show which differences are specific to the dependent sibling.

domains.note: The sibling design and the age and IQ matching address familial and some background factors, but sex, education and the siblings' own substance use are not reported in the main text, and smoking, more common in both sibling groups, was checked only for grey matter.

DSM-IV diagnosis, but the instrument, the stimulants used and any biological verification are not given in the main report; the non-dependent siblings' own drug use is defined only as no chronic abuse.
Families with a willing non-dependent sibling, and volunteer controls; recruitment is not described in the main report.
Whether the dependent siblings were using, in treatment or abstinent when scanned is not reported.
The degrees of freedom imply 144 of 150 participants analysed; the exclusions are not explained in the main text.
Automated imaging analyses and a standard computerized task.

Only the clusters shared by both sibling groups are named; group-specific clusters visible in Fig. 2 are not described, there is no direct sibling contrast, and the cluster statistics are in the supplement.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Six of seven domains raise some concerns, which together substantially lower confidence: unknown sex, education and other drug use, smoking more common in both sibling groups, six participants missing from the analyses without explanation, and a selective description of the whole-brain results. Provisional: the supplement, which was not read, may resolve the confounding, exposure and missing-data concerns. The design is a real strength for its question: differences shared with non-dependent siblings argue that part of the brain and stop-signal differences seen in stimulant dependence is familial. The study may be cited for that, with these limits; not for the claim that the differences predate use or are genetic, and not for methamphetamine specifically.

key_findings.finding: 50 sibling pairs, one sibling with DSM-IV stimulant dependence and the other with no history of chronic drug or alcohol abuse, and 50 unrelated healthy volunteers matched for age and IQ; smoking rates were higher in the sibling pairs than in the volunteers.
key_findings.note: Sample characteristics, smoking rates and drug-use data are in table S1 of the supplement, which is not in the PDF.

key_findings.finding: SSRT differed between the three groups, F(2,141) = 9.9, P < 0.001; both the dependent and the non-dependent siblings were slower than the unrelated volunteers (Bonferroni P ≤ 0.005 for both), and the non-dependent siblings' deficit was as large as the dependent siblings'.
key_findings.locator: Report text, 4th paragraph; Fig. 1A and legend
key_findings.note: Group means appear only in Fig. 1A; read from the figure (approximate): about 239 ms (controls), 277 ms (non-dependent siblings) and 280 ms (dependent siblings). The error bars are not defined in the legend.

key_findings.finding: SSRT varied less within true sibling pairs than within unrelated pairs (permutation P = 0.033), which the authors take to show a familial trait rather than a result of long-term drug use.

White-matter FA was lower in the sibling pairs than in the unrelated volunteers (tract skeleton, F(2,141) = 26.3, P < 0.001) and varied less within true sibling pairs (permutation P = 0.004); in the dependent siblings, lower FA went with longer duration of stimulant use (fig. S2A).
key_findings.note: The duration correlation is in the supplement (not read); the main report gives no statistic, only that it was less extensive anatomically than the familial effect.

key_findings.finding: Across all participants, lower FA beside the right inferior frontal gyrus went with longer SSRT, r = 0.24 (R² = 0.057, about 6% of SSRT variance, P < 0.005); this right prefrontal white matter was more alike within families than between unrelated pairs (permutation P = 0.004).
key_findings.locator: Report text, 6th paragraph; Fig. 1C and legend
key_findings.note: The correlation pools all three groups, which differ in both FA and SSRT; no within-group estimate is reported.

key_findings.finding: Grey matter: the medial temporal lobe and basal ganglia were larger in the sibling pairs than in the volunteers, and three clusters were shared by both sibling groups: a larger left amygdala and left putamen, and a smaller left postcentral gyrus, superior temporal gyrus and posterior insula.
key_findings.locator: Report text, 7th paragraph (p. 602, right column, continuing on p. 603); Fig. 2C and legend (p. 603)

key_findings.finding: The putamen enlargement (permutation P = 0.013) and the posterior insula reduction (P = 0.012) varied less within true sibling pairs than within random pairs; the amygdala enlargement did not (P = 0.144), which the authors attribute to non-familial factors.

A re-analysis restricted to non-smokers gave similar grey-matter results (fig. S1), and the grey-matter regions associated with duration of stimulant use lay in different places from the familial regions (fig. S2B).
key_findings.note: Both results are in the supplement, not read; the main report gives no statistics or region names for them.

key_findings.finding: Fig. 2A (dependent siblings against volunteers) shows several decreased-volume clusters, in ventral frontal and insular regions by the editors' reading, that do not appear in Fig. 2B (non-dependent siblings against volunteers); the text does not name, test or discuss them, and no direct comparison of the two sibling groups is reported.
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of the image; no statistics or anatomical labels are given. These may be the orbitofrontal and anterior insular reductions that London et al. (2015) describe as found only in the dependent siblings.

key_findings.finding: The authors note that the almost equal SSRT deficit in the dependent and non-dependent siblings does not follow the classic endophenotype pattern, in which relatives fall between patients and controls, and suggest that the non-dependent siblings have resilience factors.
The main report does not say which stimulants the dependent siblings used (it gives only DSM-IV dependence on stimulant drugs), nor their alcohol and other drug use or their abstinence at testing.
key_findings.note: Dean et al. (2013, p. 263) state that most participants used cocaine.

reporting_issues.issue: The SSRT and FA group comparisons are reported as F(2,141), which implies 144 participants analysed; the design has 150 (three groups of 50), and no exclusions are mentioned in the main text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Six participants are missing from these analyses without explanation; whether they came from one group, and whether the grey-matter analysis used the same 144, cannot be checked from the main report.

reporting_issues.issue: The FA–SSRT correlation is printed as r = 0.24 without a sign, while the text and Fig. 1C describe higher FA with shorter SSRT, a negative relation; R² is labelled the linear correlation constant.
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction has to be taken from the text and the figure; the value is internally consistent (0.24 squared is 0.058, printed 0.057).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports abnormalities in fronto-striatal systems in both siblings, but the grey-matter clusters shared by both (Fig. 2C) are in the left amygdala, putamen, postcentral gyrus, superior temporal gyrus and posterior insula; the only frontal finding is white matter beside the right inferior frontal gyrus.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's summary is broader than the shared grey-matter findings.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the medial temporal lobe and basal ganglia were enlarged in the sibling pairs, but the shared medial temporal cluster in Fig. 2C is the left amygdala only, and its enlargement failed the familiality test (P = 0.144); no hippocampal cluster is named.
reporting_issues.consequence: A secondary source that lists a hippocampal enlargement shared by both siblings (London et al., 2015) cannot be checked against the main report.

reporting_issues.issue: Six familiality permutation tests are reported without correction for multiple testing.
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' calculation: at a Bonferroni threshold of P < 0.0083 for six tests, the SSRT (0.033), putamen (0.013) and posterior insula (0.012) results would not be significant; only the two white-matter results (0.004) would.

reporting_issues.issue: The familiality permutation tests compare the spread within true sibling pairs with the spread within randomly re-paired participants, but the main report does not say how the random pairs were drawn or whether age and other covariates were removed first.
reporting_issues.consequence: Siblings are likely to be closer in age than randomly paired participants (editors' reasoning, not stated in the paper), and age affects white-matter FA, grey-matter volume and stop-signal performance, so part of the "familial" similarity could be shared age or shared upbringing rather than shared genes; this adds to the genes-versus-environment limit already given.

reporting_issues.issue: The FA group difference F(2,141) = 26.3 is given in the Fig. 1B legend for "the skeleton of group differences", and the region of interest for the FA–SSRT regression was then chosen inside that skeleton; the main report does not say whether the F value comes from voxels selected because they already differed between groups.
reporting_issues.consequence: If the F was computed on voxels chosen for showing a group difference, it is inflated by the selection, and the editors' FA eta-squared of about 0.27 is then too large; the pooled FA–SSRT correlation (r = 0.24) also inherits both the voxel selection and the between-group difference.

verification.checked_by: AI readers 10 and 11 (card check against the PDF) and the AI adjudicator

disagreements.reviewer: Reader 10 (missed): familiality test, p. 602 4th-6th paragraphs and p. 603 7th paragraph; the main report does not say whether age was removed before the test or how the random pairs were drawn, so shared age and environment may inflate the familial similarity.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on pp. 602-603: the permutation tests are described only as true sibling pairs versus randomly paired siblings, with no covariates or pairing procedure stated. Added as a reporting issue; the age argument is flagged as the editors' reasoning because the paper does not give the sibling age gap.

disagreements.reviewer: Reader 10 (missed): possible circular selection, Fig. 1B legend (p. 602): F(2,141) = 26.3 for the skeleton of group differences, with the right inferior frontal region of interest selected inside it; the editors' FA eta-squared should carry this caveat.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in the Fig. 1B legend and the 4th and 5th paragraphs of p. 602 (regions of interest taken within the skeleton that showed the group difference). Added as a reporting issue; the F statistic itself is unchanged and the doubt is stated conditionally because the report does not give the voxel-selection procedure.

disagreements.first_pass: about 0.12 for SSRT and 0.27 for FA.
disagreements.reviewer: Reader 10 (missed): the editors' FA eta-squared should carry the circular-selection caveat.
disagreements.resolution: Appended a conditional caveat to the editors' calculation so that the 0.27 is not read without it; the number is unchanged.
